    AI Overview
    The Iran nuclear agreement, officially known as the
    Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), was a landmark deal reached on July 14, 2015, between Iran and the P5+1 (the five permanent members of the UN Security Council—China, France, Russia, U.K., U.S.—plus Germany) and the European Union. The deal was a signature foreign policy achievement of the Obama administration, designed to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon in exchange for relief from international sanctions. 
    Core Provisions of the JCPOA 
    Under the deal, Iran agreed to major constraints on its nuclear program to increase its "breakout time"—the time needed to produce enough weapons-grade uranium for a single nuclear weapon—from two or three months to at least one year. Key actions included: 
    • Uranium Enrichment: Iran reduced its enriched uranium stockpile by 98% and capped enrichment levels at 3.67%, far below the 90% required for weapons.
    • Centrifuges: Active centrifuges were reduced by two-thirds, capped at 6,104 for ten years, with only older models allowed.
    • Plutonium Path: The Arak heavy-water reactor was redesigned to prevent it from producing weapons-grade plutonium, with spent fuel to be shipped out of the country.
    • Monitoring: The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) was granted unprecedented, intense monitoring access, including 24-hour surveillance of facilities and the ability to inspect suspicious sites.
    • Sanctions Relief: Following verification of compliance by the IAEA on "Implementation Day" (January 16, 2016), the U.S., EU, and UN lifted nuclear-related economic sanctions, allowing Iran to regain access to billions of dollars in frozen assets and international oil markets. 
    Implementation and Withdrawal (2016–2018) 
    The deal took effect on January 16, 2016. The Obama administration argued the deal offered the best path to peace, while opponents, including Israel and some U.S. lawmakers, argued it was too lenient and contained "sunset provisions" allowing restrictions to expire. 
    In May 2018, President Donald Trump withdrew the United States from the agreement, calling it "defective at its core," and reinstated heavy sanctions under a "maximum pressure" campaign. 
    Post-Obama Administration Status 
    Following the U.S. withdrawal, Iran gradually stopped complying with the restrictions in 2019, including increasing uranium enrichment to 60% and reducing IAEA access. 
    • Biden Administration: President Joe Biden expressed a willingness to return to the JCPOA if Iran returned to full compliance, but negotiations to revive the deal faced multiple delays.
    • Current Status: As of late 2023, the agreement was largely considered defunct, with Iran having accelerated its nuclear advances, bringing it closer to weapons-grade material than before the 2015 deal. 
    Note: In April 2026, amid ongoing regional tensions, it was reported that Iran officially terminated the agreement after 10 years and had accelerated its nuclear activity.
